results.name: background_set_rate_sd
results.description: Standard deviation across sets (with >=9 'background' trials: targets sharing no example's final digit and >=10 from every example) of each set's background yes-rate; observed > null means sets differ in how broadly people generalize to dissimilar numbers (set-specific rule breadth, e.g. "4,66,78,96" vs "80,70,90,100") more than the model's similarity features produce, observed < null means less.
results.code:
# name: background_set_rate_sd
# description: Standard deviation across sets (with >=9 'background' trials: targets sharing no example's final digit and >=10 from every example) of each set's background yes-rate; observed > null means sets differ in how broadly people generalize to dissimilar numbers (set-specific rule breadth, e.g. "4,66,78,96" vs "80,70,90,100") more than the model's similarity features produce, observed < null means less.
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    uniq = sets.unique()
    M = np.full((len(uniq), 4), np.nan)
    for i, s in enumerate(uniq):
        l = [int(v) for v in s.split(",")][:4]
        M[i, :len(l)] = l
    idx = pd.Series(np.arange(len(uniq)), index=uniq)[sets].to_numpy()
    E = M[idx]
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    D = np.where(np.isnan(E), np.inf, np.abs(E - t[:, None]))
    dm = ((np.nan_to_num(E, nan=-1) % 10) == (t % 10)[:, None]).any(1)
    bg = (~dm) & (D.min(1) >= 10)
    g = pd.DataFrame({"s": idx[bg], "r": r[bg]}).groupby("s")["r"].agg(["mean", "size"])
    g = g[g["size"] >= 9]
    if len(g) < 2:
        return 0.0
    return float(g["mean"].std())

results.name: single_example_shared_factor_contrast
results.description: In single-example sets, yes-rate for targets sharing a common factor >=3 with the example (gcd(target, example) >= 3, e.g. 14/49/98 for "7", 30/100 for "5") minus yes-rate for other targets; observed > null means people infer a 'multiples/factors of the example' rule from one example, which the model (no factor term for single examples) under-produces, observed < null means less.
results.code:
# name: single_example_shared_factor_contrast
# description: In single-example sets, yes-rate for targets sharing a common factor >=3 with the example (gcd(target, example) >= 3, e.g. 14/49/98 for "7", 30/100 for "5") minus yes-rate for other targets; observed > null means people infer a 'multiples/factors of the example' rule from one example, which the model (no factor term for single examples) under-produces, observed < null means less.
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    single = ~sets.str.contains(",").to_numpy()
    e = pd.to_numeric(sets.where(single, "0"), errors="coerce").fillna(0).astype(int).to_numpy()
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    g = np.gcd(e, t)
    base = single & (t != e)
    a = base & (g >= 3)
    b = base & (g < 3)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: exact_example_target_rate
results.description: Yes-rate on trials whose target equals one of the set's examples; observed < null means people endorse the shown examples less than the model's maximal self-similarity predicts (a response-noise ceiling the model lacks), observed > null means more.
results.code:
# name: exact_example_target_rate
# description: Yes-rate on trials whose target equals one of the set's examples; observed < null means people endorse the shown examples less than the model's maximal self-similarity predicts (a response-noise ceiling the model lacks), observed > null means more.
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    uniq = sets.unique()
    exs = sets.map({s: frozenset(int(v) for v in s.split(",")) for s in uniq})
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    isex = np.array([ti in e for ti, e in zip(t, exs)])
    if isex.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[isex].mean())

results.name: set_size_far_nonmatch_contrast
results.description: Among 'background' targets (share no example's final digit and lie >=10 from every example), yes-rate in sets of 3-4 examples minus in sets of 1-2 examples; observed < null means people generalize more narrowly as examples accumulate (size-principle strictness) whereas the model's summed similarity grows with more examples, observed > null means broader.
results.code:
# name: set_size_far_nonmatch_contrast
# description: Among 'background' targets (share no example's final digit and lie >=10 from every example), yes-rate in sets of 3-4 examples minus in sets of 1-2 examples; observed < null means people generalize more narrowly as examples accumulate (size-principle strictness) whereas the model's summed similarity grows with more examples, observed > null means broader.
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    uniq = sets.unique()
    M = np.full((len(uniq), 4), np.nan)
    for i, s in enumerate(uniq):
        l = [int(v) for v in s.split(",")][:4]
        M[i, :len(l)] = l
    idx = pd.Series(np.arange(len(uniq)), index=uniq)[sets].to_numpy()
    E = M[idx]
    n = (~np.isnan(E)).sum(1)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    D = np.where(np.isnan(E), np.inf, np.abs(E - t[:, None]))
    dm = ((np.nan_to_num(E, nan=-1) % 10) == (t % 10)[:, None]).any(1)
    bg = (~dm) & (D.min(1) >= 10)
    a = bg & (n >= 3)
    b = bg & (n <= 2)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: digit_match_divisor_exemption
results.description: In multi-example sets whose examples' gcd is >=3, among targets sharing some example's final digit (target not an example), yes-rate for gcd-multiples minus yes-rate for non-multiples; observed < null means people do NOT apply the common-divisor penalty to final-digit-matching targets (the digit rule overrides it, e.g. 19/59 for "69,9,39,21") while the model's constant divisor penalty does, observed > null means the divisor penalty is even stronger for them.
results.code:
# name: digit_match_divisor_exemption
# description: In multi-example sets whose examples' gcd is >=3, among targets sharing some example's final digit (target not an example), yes-rate for gcd-multiples minus yes-rate for non-multiples; observed < null means people do NOT apply the common-divisor penalty to final-digit-matching targets (the digit rule overrides it, e.g. 19/59 for "69,9,39,21") while the model's constant divisor penalty does, observed > null means the divisor penalty is even stronger for them.
def test_statistic(df):
    from math import gcd
    from functools import reduce
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    uniq = sets.unique()
    info = {s: [int(v) for v in s.split(",")] for s in uniq}
    g = sets.map({s: (reduce(gcd, l) if len(l) > 1 else 0) for s, l in info.items()}).to_numpy()
    digs = sets.map({s: frozenset(e % 10 for e in l) for s, l in info.items()})
    exs = sets.map({s: frozenset(l) for s, l in info.items()})
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    dm = np.array([(ti % 10) in dg for ti, dg in zip(t, digs)])
    isex = np.array([ti in e for ti, e in zip(t, exs)])
    base = (g >= 3) & dm & ~isex
    div = base & (t % np.maximum(g, 1) == 0)
    nd = base & (t % np.maximum(g, 1) != 0)
    if div.sum() == 0 or nd.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[div].mean() - r[nd].mean())

results.name: first_vs_last_nearest_contrast
results.description: In multi-example sets, among non-example targets, yes-rate when the magnitude-nearest example is the first one shown minus when it is the last one shown; observed > null means a primacy advantage (early examples weigh more), observed < null means a recency advantage, either of which the model's order-symmetric summed similarity cannot produce.
results.code:
# name: first_vs_last_nearest_contrast
# description: In multi-example sets, among non-example targets, yes-rate when the magnitude-nearest example is the first one shown minus when it is the last one shown; observed > null means a primacy advantage (early examples weigh more), observed < null means a recency advantage, either of which the model's order-symmetric summed similarity cannot produce.
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    uniq = sets.unique()
    M = np.full((len(uniq), 4), np.nan)
    for i, s in enumerate(uniq):
        l = [int(v) for v in s.split(",")][:4]
        M[i, :len(l)] = l
    idx = pd.Series(np.arange(len(uniq)), index=uniq)[sets].to_numpy()
    E = M[idx]
    n = (~np.isnan(E)).sum(1)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    D = np.abs(E - t[:, None])
    isex = np.nanmin(D, axis=1) == 0
    Dm = np.where(np.isnan(D), np.inf, D)
    near = np.argmin(Dm, axis=1)
    mn = Dm.min(1)
    ties = (Dm == mn[:, None]).sum(1) > 1
    base = (n >= 2) & ~isex & ~ties
    first = base & (near == 0)
    last = base & (near == n - 1)
    if first.sum() == 0 or last.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[first].mean() - r[last].mean())

results.name: digit_match_distance_corr
results.description: In multi-example sets where >=2 examples share a final digit d, among non-example targets ending in d, Pearson correlation between distance to the nearest example and the yes response; observed > null (closer to 0) means people apply the shared-digit rule flatly regardless of magnitude, whereas the model's distance-decaying similarity predicts a negative correlation; observed < null means steeper decay.
results.code:
# name: digit_match_distance_corr
# description: In multi-example sets where >=2 examples share a final digit d, among non-example targets ending in d, Pearson correlation between distance to the nearest example and the yes response; observed > null (closer to 0) means people apply the shared-digit rule flatly regardless of magnitude, whereas the model's distance-decaying similarity predicts a negative correlation; observed < null means steeper decay.
def test_statistic(df):
    from collections import Counter
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    uniq = sets.unique()
    M = np.full((len(uniq), 4), np.nan)
    rd = np.full(len(uniq), -1)
    for i, s in enumerate(uniq):
        l = [int(v) for v in s.split(",")][:4]
        M[i, :len(l)] = l
        c = Counter(e % 10 for e in l).most_common(1)[0]
        if len(l) >= 2 and c[1] >= 2:
            rd[i] = c[0]
    idx = pd.Series(np.arange(len(uniq)), index=uniq)[sets].to_numpy()
    E = M[idx]
    d = rd[idx]
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    D = np.where(np.isnan(E), np.inf, np.abs(E - t[:, None])).min(1)
    m = (d >= 0) & ((t % 10) == d) & (D > 0)
    if m.sum() < 3:
        return 0.0
    x, y = D[m], r[m]
    if x.std() == 0 or y.std() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(np.corrcoef(x, y)[0, 1])

results.name: background_trial_drift_corr
results.description: Among 'background' targets (share no example's final digit and lie >=10 from every example), Pearson correlation between trial_index and the yes response; observed > null means the low-similarity yes floor rises over the session (growing guessing/lapse or loosening), observed < null means it falls, which the stationary model cannot produce.
results.code:
# name: background_trial_drift_corr
# description: Among 'background' targets (share no example's final digit and lie >=10 from every example), Pearson correlation between trial_index and the yes response; observed > null means the low-similarity yes floor rises over the session (growing guessing/lapse or loosening), observed < null means it falls, which the stationary model cannot produce.
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    uniq = sets.unique()
    M = np.full((len(uniq), 4), np.nan)
    for i, s in enumerate(uniq):
        l = [int(v) for v in s.split(",")][:4]
        M[i, :len(l)] = l
    idx = pd.Series(np.arange(len(uniq)), index=uniq)[sets].to_numpy()
    E = M[idx]
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    D = np.where(np.isnan(E), np.inf, np.abs(E - t[:, None]))
    dm = ((np.nan_to_num(E, nan=-1) % 10) == (t % 10)[:, None]).any(1)
    bg = (~dm) & (D.min(1) >= 10)
    x = df["trial_index"].astype(float).to_numpy()[bg]
    y = r[bg]
    if len(y) < 3 or x.std() == 0 or y.std() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(np.corrcoef(x, y)[0, 1])
